source.reasoning_observation: Transverse motion of string and airborne longitudinal sound differ; common frequency does not imply equal wavelength. Publisher key D accepts an amplitude-squared loudness assertion; physically, intensity scales with pressure amplitude squared under matched impedance, while perceived loudness is not generally proportional and string-to-air coupling matters. Flag for R01.

target.protected_work: Evaluate claims of equal wavelength and amplitude-based loudness by constructing compatible countermodels and identifying independent measurements of coupling and propagation.
target.decisive_route: Two sources have same measured string displacement amplitude but one radiates twice the pressure amplitude at a matched sensor. Can equal string amplitude prove equal intensity? Shortest valid route: No; different coupling gives different pressure. At same impedance, intensity ratio4, but loudness not fixed.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Distinguish string transverse motion, airborne longitudinal propagation and perception.

representation_translation.evidence: Relate same-frequency boundary coupling to different medium wave speeds.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Construct counterexamples and discriminating calibrated measurements.

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Intensity proportionality does not establish perceived loudness or universal string coupling.

core1a.scientific_construction: An ideal stretched string supports transverse displacement waves. It can drive air through its motion and a sounding body, generating longitudinal pressure disturbances. At a stationary coupling boundary driven periodically, the transmitted tone can share the source frequency while its wavelength changes because λ=v/f and wave speeds in string and air differ. The string displacement amplitude is not the airborne pressure amplitude. In a linear progressive sinusoidal acoustic field of fixed impedance Z, time-averaged intensity is p_peak²/(2Z); if pressure amplitude doubles at unchanged Z, intensity quadruples. The coupling from string displacement to pressure depends on frequency, geometry, damping, direction and radiation. Perceived loudness is not a universal linear function of intensity. A school-level amplitude-squared statement needs an explicitly limited physical model; keep publisher key unchanged and distinguish measured quantities.

worked_anchor.task: A string supports a 200 Hz wave at100 m/s; airborne tone has speed340 m/s. Compare wavelengths.
worked_anchor.reasoning: String 0.5 m; air1.7 m. Common frequency does not make wavelengths equal.

core1a.model_limits: Only specified ideal/matched conditions; extension relations are supplied, not independently warranted compulsory syllabus scope.

core1b.task: Two sounding boards carry identical strings whose measured periodic motions have equal frequency and equal displacement amplitude. One board produces a calibrated microphone pressure amplitude twice the other at the same location in the same air. A report states the strings must have different frequencies and the louder board's wave must have twice the wavelength. Evaluate the claims, construct a consistent alternative and identify measurements that could test it.
core1b.protected_work: Evaluate claims of equal wavelength and amplitude-based loudness by constructing compatible countermodels and identifying independent measurements of coupling and propagation.

stages.reconstruct: Same measured f and same air speed imply same airborne λ; changed coupling may double pressure without frequency change. Under matched linear progressive conditions intensity ratio4, not automatically perceived loudness ratio. Measure source motion, air speed, calibrated pressure and angular/field response.
stages.diagnose: Identify confusion between source displacement, sound pressure, intensity and loudness, or between shared frequency and wavelength.
stages.repair: Label each medium and measured variable, calculate λ separately, compare calibrated intensities only under stated impedance and field assumptions.
stages.boundary_test: If the microphones are in different gases with unknown impedances, can pressure ratio alone establish intensity ratio4?

core1b.boundary_response_criterion: No; I_A/I_B=4Z_B/Z_A under stated acoustic model.

core1b.task: A string wave and radiated airborne tone have common frequency 250 Hz. String speed125 m/s; air speed350 m/s. Two configurations use the same string displacement amplitude but different sounding bodies, with pressure amplitudes 3 and 6 Pa in matched progressive air fields. A student claims the wavelengths are equal and the second configuration is four times as loud. Assess both claims and state a defensible quantitative conclusion.
